title: KV cache telemetry, TTL drift, and prefix-shadow troubleshooting
meeting_header: Date: 2025-05-15 | Start: 14:30 UTC | Duration: 73 min | Recording: link.redwood/ff/9834 | Attendees: Eli Navarro (Redwood), Monica Chen (Redwood SE), Dr. Aisha Rahman (Pinecrest ML), Tom Hernandez (Platform), Sofia Vega (SRE)
summary: SE-led deep dive on observed KV cache instability: high eviction spikes during mixed short/long context workloads. Discussed telemetry signals, root causes (prefix shadowing, TTL drift, batch-induced thrash), mitigations (pinning, tiered TTLs, spillback tuning, prefetching), and next steps to run targeted benchmarks on Pinecrest's on-prem cluster.
topics: KV cache eviction policies and telemetry
paging (spill to host/NVMe) and spillback behavior
long-context sessions and prefix reuse patterns
VPC/on-prem monitoring constraints and kernel mismatch risks
action_items: Eli Navarro: Share current KV eviction dashboard + sample query to compute prefix reuse rate (due: 2025-05-20)
Monica Chen: Provide small repro harness (container) that reproduces eviction spike on 8xA100 on-prem (due: 2025-05-22)
Tom Hernandez: Export workload trace (2 hours) with token timestamps and batching rates and upload to secure S3 (due: 2025-05-19)
Sofia Vega: Confirm KMS/HSM constraints for on-prem profiling (due: 2025-05-21)
next_steps: Redwood to run KV-aware profiler against Pinecrest trace in staging and produce a heatmap of prefix occupancy over time
Customer to run a canary with pinned prefixes for critical long-context flows next week
Schedule follow-up 30-min check-in after profiler run (tentative: 2025-05-27)
transcript:
[00:00] Eli Navarro: alright hi everyone, thanks for joining — we'll kick off the deep dive on the KV cache behavior you reported. Monica is going to lead. um quick roll call?
[00:12] Monica Chen: hey all, Monica Chen here, I'm the SE on inference runtime. Eli is on the account side.
[00:18] Aisha Rahman: Hi, Aisha — ML lead at Pinecrest. We saw intermittent latency spikes and a rise in out-of-memory-like eviction errors on our Redwood Dedicated nodes.
[00:27] Tom Hernandez: Tom here, platform eng. We run a mix of short chat queries and long doc summarization sessions. The problem looks correlated with mixed traffic.
[00:36] Monica Chen: yeah ok. before we jump in, quick framing: we typically see two classes of issues — steady-state misses due to prefix variety, and transient thrash where batching + eviction collide. We'll go through telemetry and then repro ideas.
[00:50] Eli Navarro: tiny note, some of the logs you sent labeled things as "kv spillback" and "cache eviction" interchangeably — they're related but distinct ops, just want the nomenclature clear.
[01:02] Sofia Vega: yeah and we saw "spill-to-host" events in the logs at 03:14 UTC — that corresponded to a 500ms tail latency blip.
[01:12] Monica Chen: perfect, that's a good anchor. ok, starting with architecture recap — our KV cache is per-model-shard LRU-ish with configurable TTL and an eviction governor that tries to avoid evicting prefixes currently in use. Good to remember that some model variants create larger KV entries because of different kv-layouts after quantization.
[01:36] Aisha Rahman: quick question — could quantization change the size such that entries exceed slot expectations and trigger earlier eviction?
[01:43] Monica Chen: yes, especially for 8-bit quant profiles where the tensor packing changes; we've seen effective entry sizes vary by ~20-30% between float16 and q8 variants. so if your fleet mixes variants, partitioning matters.
[01:55] Tom Hernandez: that might be us — we left sim-different variants for warm start experiments.
[02:02] Monica Chen: ok noted. telemetry you should look for: eviction_rate per-shard, spill_to_host_rate, prefix_miss_rate, prefix_reuse_count, active_slot_occupancy, and the governor backoff counter. Also token-latency breakdown per-batch-size.
[02:20] Eli Navarro: can we surface prefix-level TTLs in your dashboards? we noticed TTL drift in one of the traces where TTLs shortened unexpectedly.
[02:28] Monica Chen: TTL drift usually happens when a prefix is touched by an inferred "refresh" path that reinserts with a shorter TTL or when pinned markers get dropped after restarts. In Redwood Dedicate — sorry Redwood Dedicated — we ship a pinned-prefix flag that survives soft restarts, but not hard node reprovisioning unless you persist the marker externally.
[02:48] Sofia Vega: hm we do node reprovs during patch windows. that could explain the shorter lived pins.
[02:55] Monica Chen: yep. next, prefix-shadowing — this is when near-identical prompt prefixes (small token differences, e.g., user metadata appended) create many distinct keys that occupy slots and prevent reuse. In your trace we saw a high cardinality of prefixes for the same logical flow.
[03:14] Aisha Rahman: that's probably our multi-tenant templating layer — we append session-id for traceability and forgot to mask it before caching.
[03:22] Monica Chen: yep that will destroy reuse. short term, you can perform prefix normalization/masking in your prompt pipeline or on the Redwood side we can introduce a hashing filter to collapse session suffixes, but that requires coordination for correctness.
[03:36] Tom Hernandez: is there an automatic prefetch hook? so when a long-context session appears we prime the likely next prefixes?
[03:44] Monica Chen: we have a prefetcher in the runtime — it can be trained on observed transition patterns and run as a heuristic. But in on-prem/VPC setups with restricted profiling, we need your permission to ship aggregated transition stats or run a local offline profiler.
[03:59] Eli Navarro: Monica, can you walk through one of the eviction spike sequences in the trace?
[04:05] Monica Chen: sure. looking at 03:13:50 UTC: concurrent batch peak at 64 tokens per request, batching window ~12ms, induced a bunch of new prefixes (short chat completions) while two long-context jobs touched long prefix chains. The eviction governor saw occupancy hit 98%, started evicting least-recently-used, but because many of the long-context prefixes were recently referenced by the long sessions they weren't technically LRU — instead we saw "epoch eviction" where the governor moves whole slab ranges to host to free contiguous memory. That spilled back to CPU and NVMe which increased tail latencies.
[04:41] Sofia Vega: can you expand on "epoch eviction"? that's a new term for us.
[04:45] Monica Chen: it's our name for slab-level reclamation that reduces fragmentation. It trades more throughput for lower fragmentation. But if your workload mixes tiny short-lived prefixes and long chains, epoch eviction can prematurely move active kvs if the slab heuristics mis-classify hotness.
[05:01] Tom Hernandez: ok, so how do we detect that misclassification preemptively?
[05:06] Monica Chen: key signals: sudden jump in slab_move_count, host_spill_bytes rising, prefix_reuse_rate dropping, and a surge in small-batch arrivals. We can create a composite alert.
[05:18] Aisha Rahman: what about adjusting TTLs? we have different SLAs per route — if we raise TTLs, won't that cause memory pressure?
[05:25] Monica Chen: yes it's a balancing act. recommended pattern: tiered TTLs — short TTL for highly variable short-chat prefixes, medium TTL for sessions, long TTL for pinned prefixes used by multi-turn long-context flows. The runtime supports per-route TTL overrides and dynamic TTL backoff under high pressure (reduces TTL adaptively).
[05:44] Eli Navarro: you mentioned pinned prefixes earlier. what's the cost of pinning too many?
[05:49] Monica Chen: pinned prefixes bypass eviction which increases guaranteed memory usage. If you pin too many you'll force slab expansions or more frequent epochs. So pin only the top N critical flows (we saw best results pinning <1% of unique prefixes for most customers).
[06:01] Tom Hernandez: and prefix reuse — is it safe to canonicalize prompts to increase reuse? we worry about breaking downstream analytics that rely on session ids.
[06:09] Monica Chen: you can have both — canonicalize to the cache key but keep session-id in a separate metadata header for logging. That way analytics remain intact.
[06:18] Aisha Rahman: earlier you said quantization changes KV layout. can that interact with eviction patterns across different shards?
[06:24] Monica Chen: yes. quantized kernels produce different kv sizes and different memory alignment. If you mix variants on the same physical pool, the allocator sees heterogeneous object sizes and fragmentation goes up. Recommendation: partition by quant profile or run homogeneous pools per shard.
[06:39] Eli Navarro: what about batching? we sometimes bump batch windows to save cost. Are we increasing eviction risk?
[06:46] Monica Chen: larger batches increase simultaneous KV generations which temporarily boost occupancy; if the governor's smoothing window is too short, you'll get an eviction spike. So we suggest smoothing the governor window or applying burst buffers. Also, small increases in batch size combined with high concurrency cause more prefix churn.
[07:03] Tom Hernandez: is there a safe way to test changes without impacting production?
[07:07] Monica Chen: run a synthetic replay of your trace against a staging Dedicated node with identical shard config. We can provide a lightweight harness that injects the same batching and token timing. Monica will share that container.
[07:18] Aisha Rahman: regarding telemetry, can Redwood ship aggregate prefix-heatmaps? we can't share raw tokens.
[07:24] Monica Chen: yes, we can run the profiler in your VPC and produce aggregated heatmaps without exporting raw content. We'll mark it as a secure on-prem profiling job. Eli will coordinate with Sofia for KMS access.
[07:36] Sofia Vega: KMS/HSM team will need the job spec. We can't allow any persistent keys to leave the cluster.
[07:42] Eli Navarro: understood. Monica, any quick remediation we can try today?
[07:46] Monica Chen: three quick things: 1) apply prompt normalization to strip session suffixes, 2) pin the top 0.5% of prefixes identified in your recent 24h trace, 3) lower the epoch eviction aggressiveness parameter from default to conservative. We'll send commands for these.
[08:02] Tom Hernandez: can we also get a list of runtime flags that affect slab behavior and their safe ranges?
[08:08] Monica Chen: yes — I'll include the flags doc. Key ones: slab_reclaim_threshold, epoch_eviction_enabled, epoch_aggressiveness (0-10), host_spill_backoff_ms, ttl_adaptive_enabled.
[08:20] Aisha Rahman: cool. one more question about long context — sometimes the long sessions show prefix reuse but still get evicted mid-session. Is that likely a restart or fragmentation?
[08:29] Monica Chen: mid-session evictions are almost always either pinned marker loss on node restart, or if the long context is stored across multiple shards and one shard evicted while others didn't, causing an inconsistent full-kv snapshot. We added cross-shard consistency checks but they can be disabled in low-latency modes.
[08:46] Eli Navarro: any tradeoffs to re-enabling the consistency checks?
[08:50] Monica Chen: small latency tax — ~5-10ms per token in worst cases — but it prevents partial cache corruption for long contexts.
[08:58] Aisha Rahman: ok that's probably worth it for our long-doc workflows.
[09:02] Monica Chen: noted.
[09:05] Monica Chen: next, quantization interactions — if you're using mixed precisions for A/B tests, watch for inter-shard eviction correlates. We can surface cross-variant eviction heatmaps.
[09:16] Tom Hernandez: speaking of heatmaps, what's the easiest metric to compute client-side to approximate prefix reuse?
[09:21] Monica Chen: compute reuse as distinct_prefixes / total_requests over a window; lower ratio -> better reuse. Also compute conditional reuse by route. We'll share a Grafana snippet.
[09:31] Eli Navarro: great. let's talk about paging and NVMe — you mentioned spillback tuning earlier.
[09:36] Monica Chen: spillback is our mechanism to move cold slabs to host or NVMe. If NVMe throughput is constrained, you'll see queueing causing tail latencies. Increase host_spill_workers or prioritize async writes to thin clients. But beware writes can saturate PCIe in older on-prem boxes.
[09:51] Sofia Vega: our on-prem nodes are a mix — some older 40GB PCIe lanes. we'll need a compatibility run.
[09:58] Monica Chen: ok we should run a stress test to measure spill throughput. We'll include an nvme-simulator option in the harness.
[10:05] Aisha Rahman: are there any known bugs that produce false eviction logs? one of our logs shows eviction_reason="inactive" but reuse shortly after.
[10:14] Monica Chen: sometimes the governor mislabels events when a slab move is in progress — the entry can be evicted from GPU and rehydrated from host rapidly, which shows as eviction followed by immediate miss/hit. We'll check if your runtime version has the recent fix for quick-rehydration labels.
[10:28] Eli Navarro: Monica, could you summarize the immediate mitigation path we agreed on?
[10:32] Monica Chen: sure: 1) prefix normalization to reduce cardinality, 2) pin critical long-context prefixes, 3) conservative epoch_eviction setting, 4) run Redwood profiler in VPC to generate heatmaps, 5) staging replay with matching batch/timing.
[10:45] Aisha Rahman: ok we'll get Tom and Sofia to run the trace export by Monday.
[10:49] Tom Hernandez: yes, we'll export the 2-hour window and redact tokens.
[10:53] Sofia Vega: I'll coordinate KMS constraints and open a specimen ticket for the profiling job.
[10:59] Eli Navarro: perfect. Monica, any doc links or decks to share after?
[11:03] Monica Chen: I'll share the KV quickstart guide, flags cheat-sheet, and a sample repro container. expect a follow-up email with attachments.
[11:11] Aisha Rahman: thanks everyone.
[11:14] Monica Chen: thanks — we'll reconvene after the profiler run.
[11:18] [END OF TRANSCRIPT — timestamps truncated for brevity; full raw logs are available in recording link]
